Dr. Leo can put everything back where it belongs — and your horse can undo half of it by nightfall if you're not careful.

The adjustment is the easy part. What happens in the next 24 hours determines whether it holds.

Three things that pull North Texas horses backward before their next run:

— Loping hard the same day. Let the joints settle.
— Loading straight into a trailer. Road vibration is real.
— Waiting three months and calling it maintenance.

If your horse is competing regularly, the work between sessions matters as much as the session itself. Dr. Leo will walk you through the whole picture when he's at your barn.

Pinning ears at the saddle. Ducking off pattern. Won't rate. Won't collect.

Every trainer in DFW has seen it. Half the time it gets labeled a mindset problem. Sold to a greener rider. Hauled to a trainer.

Sometimes it's behavior. But a horse that's sore behind, locked in the pelvis, or tight through the poll will show you every one of those symptoms — and no amount of riding fixes a structural problem.

Dr. Leo has put hands on horses that were days from being sold. They left moving like a different animal.

If your horse has changed — not dramatically, just a little off, a little resistant — it's worth a look before you write it off.

DM us to book. We're running North Texas.

A long haul doesn't hurt your horse the way a wreck does. It's quieter than that.

Hours of bracing against the trailer, holding balance, absorbing road. By the time you park, she looks fine. Eats. Drinks. Acts normal.

Then you run her and something's just a little off. Stride isn't even. Stop isn't digging. She's running past the first barrel.

That's the haul talking.

Dr. Leo works with performance horses all across North Texas who haul hard and compete often. Getting evaluated after a long trip — before the next run — is one of the highest-return things you can do for a horse that's on the road all season.
